title: The sack of Rome by the Visigoths
subject: histoire
description: In August 410, Alaric's Visigoths looted Rome for three days. For the first time in eight centuries, an enemy army walked into the Eternal City.

hero.hook: In 410, Rome fell. And with it, the idea of an empire that could not be beaten.

blocks.text: In August **410**, the unthinkable happened. Led by their king **Alaric**, the **Visigoths**, a Germanic people, forced the gates of Rome. For the first time since the Gallic sack of **390 BC**, nearly **800 years** earlier, an enemy army plundered the Eternal City.
Rome was no longer the political capital of the Empire, but it was still its symbolic heart. The shock exposed a truth nobody wanted to see: the Roman West was dying.

At the start of the 5th century, the Western Roman Empire was short of money and short of soldiers. To hold its borders, it signed more and more treaties of the kind known as the [[Roman foedus]]: peoples the Romans called “barbarians” settled inside the Empire in exchange for military service. The Roman machine still turned, but it now leaned on the very peoples it had once struggled to keep out.

In **402**, the Western emperor [[Honorius]] left Rome for [[Ravenna]], an Italian city protected by its marshes. While the court sheltered behind the swamps, the Roman aristocracy went on living as if nothing had changed. Real power slipped toward generals of Germanic origin.
When Honorius was told that “Rome” had fallen, he is said to have panicked: he thought it meant his favorite hen, which carried that name. He was reportedly relieved to hear it was “only” the city.

[[Alaric I]] was no savage out of nowhere. A former officer of the Roman army, pushed west by the [[Huns]], a nomadic people from Asia, he wanted land and an official title for his people. Met with contempt from Ravenna, he used Rome as a hostage. Two sieges, ransoms, then the assault.

blocks.caption: Alaric I, king of the Visigoths and a former Roman officer

blocks.text: On **August 24, 410**, the Salarian Gate swung open. The looting lasted **three days**. Alaric was an [[Arian]] Christian, from a branch of the faith that did not see Christ as the equal of God the Father, and he ordered his men to respect the churches as places of sanctuary. The violence was real, but it was not total destruction: he saw himself as the heir of Rome, not its gravedigger.
Legend says that when he died, his men diverted the river Busento to bury Alaric and his treasure, then let the water flow back over the grave.

sections.title: The shock and The City of God

blocks.text: From Palestine, [[Saint Jerome]], a Father of the Church, cried out: “In one city, the whole world has perished.” Pagans blamed Christianity for weakening Rome. To answer them, **Saint Augustine** wrote [[The City of God]]: earthly empires pass away, while the Church endures.

blocks.caption: The sack of Rome in 410, a shock to the whole ancient world

blocks.text: The signal was clear to other Germanic peoples, such as the [[Vandals]] and the [[Franks]]: the West was prey. In **455**, the Vandals sacked Rome far more brutally. In **476**, the [[Heruli]] chieftain [[Odoacer]] deposed the last Western emperor, [[Romulus Augustulus]]. The imperial insignia were shipped to Constantinople. The Western Empire was over.

sections.title: The turn toward the Middle Ages

blocks.text: The Visigoths eventually settled in Aquitaine, then in Hispania, present-day Spain. They did not wipe out classical culture. They carried it forward, blending Roman law, Christian faith and Germanic tradition.

The sack of **410** is the break that stayed in people's memory. It was not yet the administrative end of the Empire, but it was the end of the illusion. Medieval Europe began in the rubble of a myth.
In **410**, Rome fell for the first time in **800 years**. Visigoths trained the Roman way looted it for three days. The shock opened the road to **476** and to medieval Europe.
